name: Abulas
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Wearne, Helen & Pat Wilson. 1970. Abulas phonemes. Unpublished ms., 62 pp. Ukarumpa: Summer Institute of Linguistics (SIL Language & Culture Archives 31151; former SIL-PNG id 50782). Maprik dialect. Corroborated by SIL-PNG, Organised Phonology Data: Ambulas [ABT] (data checked by Pat Wilson 1992/1996), p.4; second primary for the Wosera dialect: Laycock, Donald C. 1965. catalog_locator: sec. 5.3.1 'Phonemic Status of Stress and Length', p.31. OPD: p.4. Laycock: pp.29-30 (sec. 5.21-5.24.3); Laycock stress examples checked on p.30 (accents are lost).
catalog_quote: 5.3.1. Phonemic Status of Stress and Length. Stress tends to occur on the second last syllable of the word. In a four syllable word, however, there may be light stress on both the first and third syllables. There seems to be a change of stress when there is a change of intonation or focus. /nɨwa/ ('nɨwʌ) mother; /bwiyak/ ('mbwiyʌk) rat; /vaatkna/ ('va·t·knʌ) cricket; /abutak/ (ʌ'mbutʰʌk) frog sp.; /kaawiya/ (kʰa'wiyʌ) grub; /pustakna/ (pus'tʰəknʌ) fold over; /akitawe/ ('ʌkʰi'tʰəwe) put foot up on something; /mulaskwiwu/ ('mulʌs'kwiwu) woman's name; /kelakɨtkɨ/ ('kʰelə'kʰɨtkʰɨ) will seize. The names of trees and birds tend to be stressed of [sic] the last syllable. /maasa/ (ma'sʌ) betel nut; /apwidi/ (ʌpwi'ndi) banana sp.; /sɨbwiya/ (sɨbwi'yʌ) tree sp.; ... /kwumun/ (kwu'mun) bird sp.; /manɨwi/ (mənɨ'wi) bird sp. Word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress which is often accompanied by length and often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus. /nɨwa/ ('nɨwʌ) mother; /nɨwa lɨ ro/ (nɨ'wʌ· lɨ ro) mother she sits; /pwepwe/ ('pwepwe) bat sp.; /pwepwe lɨ yu/ (pwe'pwe li yu) bat sp. she goes; /mwitɨk/ ('mwitʰɨk) good, well; /mwitɨk dɨ tu/ (mwi'tʰɨk dɨ tu) well he stands. [OPD p.4: 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) / Stress usually occurs on the second last syllable.']

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (62 pp scan, no text; the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Abulas phonemes', Keywords '50782; abt'). I rendered p.32 at 150 dpi and read the page scan myself. The TOC (p.2, printed p.1) lists '5.3. Supra-segmental Features.. 31', so p.32 = printed p.31 as the locator says. The page is headed '5.3. Supra-segmental Items. / 5.3.1. Phonemic Status of Stress and Length.' and reads: 'Stress tends to occur on the second last syllable of the word. In a four syllable word, however, there may be light stress on both the first and third syllables. There seems to be a change of stress when there is a change of intonation or focus.' [examples 'nɨwʌ mother, mbwi'yʌk rat, 'va·t·knʌ cricket,…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and by default penultimate (confirmed by the SIL OPD 1992/96: 'Stress usually occurs on the second last syllable'); in four-syllable words light stresses fall on the 1st and 3rd (i.e. alternating, penult still prominent); a lexical class (tree and bird names) tends to final stress; some disyllables with a closed final syllable are transcribed with final stress (mbwi'yʌk 'rat'), matching Laycock's 1965 Wosera rule that a closed second syllable attracts stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Wearne & Wilson: four-syllable words may have light stress on both first and third syllables ('ʌkʰi'tʰəwe, 'mulʌs'kwiwu). Laycock 1965 (Wosera): secondary stress on any nucleus adjacent to the primary if of equal rank, and iteratively re-applied after an unstressed nucleus, so no more than three unstressed nuclei in a row.
new_statements.exceptions: Names of trees and birds tend to final stress (ma'sʌ 'betel nut', kwu'mun 'bird sp.'); closed final syllables can carry stress in disyllables; Laycock 1965 pp.29-30 instead analyses Wosera-dialect stress as weight/quality-sensitive within the first two syllables of the phonological phrase (higher-ranking nucleus wins; ties go to the first syllable in disyllables unless the second is closed, otherwise to the second syllable), with phrase-final open syllables never stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tendency stated on citation forms; both W&W and Laycock say word stress yields to phrase stress: W&W 'word stress tends to be lost to phrase stress.. often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus' (nɨ'wʌ· lɨ ro 'mother she sits' vs 'nɨwʌ 'mother'); Laycock defines stress over the phonological phrase (one primary stress per pause-free stretch). W&W and Wilson describe the Maprik (northern, Samu-Kundi) dialect; Laycock the Wosera (Kamu-Kundi) dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Wearne & Wilson 1970, the SIL OPD and Wilson 1980 describe the Maprik (northern, 'Samu-Kundi') dialect of Ambulas (data mainly from Yamikum village); Laycock 1965 describes the Wosera ('Kamu-Kundi') dialect recorded at Kunjingini, which Glottolog/Ethnologue keep inside Ambulas [abt] ambu1247 (distinct from Hanga Hundi/West Wosera [wos]). The two dialect descriptions give different formulations of the stress rule (penult tendency vs. nucleus-rank-sensitive within the first two syllables of the phrase).

new_statements.quote: [Suppl. p.10, PDF p.56:] Stress, length and pitch are non-contrastive on the phonological word level. [...] Phonological words are usually pronounced with stress on the second last syllable. In words of 3 - 5 syllables if /ɨ/ is the vowel of the second last syllable the stress tends to change back to the third last syllable. Syllables preceding stress tend to be of equal light stress and length and syllables following stress are unstressed and often faster in speed. [Suppl. p.14, PDF p.60:] General Rule - Stress falls on the second last syllable. If the word contains more than five syllables a secondary stress falls on the fourth or fifth last syllable.
new_statements.citation: Wearne, Helen and Wilson, Pat (2008 [1970]). Ambulas phonemes.

All read from page scan.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened and rendered pp.3, 32, 45, 46, 56, 60, 61, 62 as images and read them. p.56 = 'Supplement to Abulas Phonemes p.10, Suprasegmental Features (replacing pp.31, 32)': 'Stress, length and pitch are non-contrastive on the phonological word level.' and item 3 'Phonological words are usually pronounced with stress on the second last syllable. In words of 3 - 5 syllables if /ɨ/ is the vowel of the second last syllable the stress tends to change back to the third last syllable. Syllables preceding stress tend to be of equal light stress and length and syllables following stress are unstressed and often faster in speed.' -- verbatim as quoted. p.60 = suppl. p.14 'Phonological word stress rules'…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog rule (penultimate stress = penultimate) and the existing 1970 p.31 statement, but the previously unread January 1977 supplement (same PDF, pp. 56-61) states explicitly that stress is non-contrastive, gives a secondary-stress rule for >5-syllable words, a vowel-quality retraction rule (/ɨ/ penult -> antepenult) and suffix-conditioned final-stress cases, all of which the catalog does not record.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls by default on the penultimate syllable; it retracts to the antepenult when the penult vowel is the short high central /ɨ/ (in 3-syllable words also when the penult has /i/ or /u/, or in the vowel sequences V1=aa/e + V2=a); certain verb suffixes shift it (-k, -n: final unless /ɨ/; -u, -o: final); words of more than five syllables get a secondary stress on the 4th- or 5th-last syllable; phrase stress overrides word stress. The original 1970 text (p.31) said the same in weaker form: 'Stress tends to occur on the second last syllable of the word', with tree and bird names stressed on the last syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Suppl. p.14: 'If the word contains more than five syllables a secondary stress falls on the fourth or fifth last syllable'; suppl. p.15: verb endings -u, -o take 'stress on final syllable and light stress on third or fourth last syllable'; original p.31: 'In a four syllable word, however, there may be light stress on both the first and third syllables'; suppl. p.10: syllables preceding stress carry 'equal light stress and length'.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) /ɨ/ in the penult of 3-5 syllable words retracts stress to the antepenult (and for nouns + -ba 'from' in 3-syllable combinations); (b) 3-syllable words with /i/ or /u/ in the penult, or with V1 aa/e + V2 a, retract to the antepenult; (c) 2-syllable words may have even stress on both syllables, and verbs with /aa/ in the last syllable stress it; (d) verb roots with relational suffixes: -ka/-kɨ/-kwa/-ye retract if the penult has /ɨ/ (but -bɨt 'they two' takes the stress); -ran/-ɨte/-ute/-katik give antepenult; -k/-n give final stress unless the final has /ɨ/ (but du-dɨ takes the stress); -u/-o give final stress; (e) compound verbs stay separate phonological words; /awu/, /awa/, /ayɨ/ count as one syllable; (f) original 1970 p.31: names of trees and birds stressed on the last syllable; word stress 'tends to be lost to phrase stress which.. often falls on the last syllable of the word in focus'.
new_statements.identity_note: Wearne & Wilson describe the Abulas of the Maprik Sub-district (East Sepik), i.e. the Maprik dialect; the 1977 supplement was written 'after a dialect survey' (Wilson 1976). Draper & Draper 1968 is by title Maprik-dialect material, and Kundama, Sapai & Wilson 1987 is the Maprik-dialect triglot dictionary (Glottolog rec. 78625). Laycock 1965 (earlier reading) treats the Wosera dialect.

sources.note: 'Stress is non-phonemic, being wholly conditioned by the syllable and nuclear structure of the phrase.' Primary stress falls on the higher-ranking nucleus (complex aw/ay > simple; a > ʌ > ə) of the first two nuclei of the phonological phrase; if equal in rank the first N is stressed unless the second syllable is closed or the phrase has more than two syllables, in which case the second N is stressed; a phrase-final open syllable is always unstressed; secondary stress on adjacent equal-rank N and iteratively after an unstressed N. Examples: /mə́nə/ 'you', /kə́pma/ 'ground' vs /vətɨ́k/ 'two', /…
